title: A man floating in empty air was Avicenna’s argument for the soul
body: In the early 11th century, the Persian philosopher Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, asked readers to imagine a person created fully formed but suspended in the air, unable to see, limbs held apart, sensing nothing at all. Such a person, he argued, would still be aware that they exist, so the self must be distinct from the body. Scholars debate how closely Descartes’s ‘I think, therefore I am’ echoes the idea six centuries later.

slides.heading: The floating man, step by step

steps.label: A person is created adult, floating in air
No sight, no touch: not one sensation
Would they still affirm that they exist? Yes
So the self is known apart from the body

slides.question: Cut off from every sensation, what would the floating man still know, according to Avicenna?
slides.explanation: Avicenna argued that such a person would still be aware of existing, so the self must be distinct from the body.
